The reproductive biology of Parore (Girella tricuspidata) has been investigated in several field studies along the eastern Australian coastline, with particular attention to the seasonal timing of spawning and the condition of mature individuals. During the peak of the spawning season, gravid females exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 5.5% [GSI = 5.5%] when measured at a water temperature of 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C]. This moderate index suggests an iteroparous reproductive strategy in which resources are partitioned across multiple annual spawning events rather than being allocated to a single, high-effort bout. The regional thermal regime appears to exert a strong influence on the onset and duration of gonadal recrudescence, with the 16.6 °C condition representing an average ambient temperature during the active spawning window in temperate New South Wales estuaries. Such thermal dependence is consistent with patterns observed in other Girella species inhabiting similar latitudinal ranges, where reproductive activity is confined to a narrow window of stable water temperatures.

Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses of wild-caught individuals indicate that Parore reaches a maximum recorded total length of 71 centimeters [Li = 71 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the family Kyphosidae. This ultimate total length is attained only after many years of sustained somatic expansion, reflecting the species' relatively slow but determinate growth pattern. In contrast, the onset of reproductive competence is marked by a considerably smaller body size, with the total length at puberty estimated at 29.5 centimeters [Lp = 29.5 centimeters] from field collections of individuals exhibiting the first macroscopic signs of gonadal development. The gap between these two length thresholds implies an extended juvenile phase during which energy is channeled primarily into structural growth and the accumulation of lipid reserves necessary for future reproductive effort. Comparable length-based maturity schedules have been reported for congeneric species from the western Pacific, suggesting a conserved life-history strategy within the genus Girella.

Early life stages in Parore are characterized by a very small starting mass, reflecting the modest size of the pelagic eggs from which they hatch. Based on an average egg diameter of 1.2 millimeters and assuming spherical geometry, the wet weight at birth is calculated to be approximately 0.0009 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0009 grams], a value that underscores the extreme vulnerability of newly emerged prolarvae. This minute initial mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for marine teleost hatchlings, necessitating a rapid transition to exogenous feeding before yolk reserves become exhausted. The yolk-sac larva period is therefore brief, and successful recruitment depends critically on the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey in the water column at the moment of first exogenous feeding. Any mismatch between hatching phenology and local zooplankton blooms can result in high mortality rates during this early developmental window, a bottleneck that likely shapes broader population dynamics in variable coastal environments.

At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight for Parore has been calculated from the length-weight relationship derived from extensive local sampling, yielding a maximum adult body mass of 4300 grams [Wwi = 4300 grams]. This upper mass threshold corresponds to the largest recorded individuals and provides a benchmark for assessing the physiological condition of older adults within the population. In contrast, individuals just reaching reproductive maturity weigh approximately 297.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 297.5 grams] based on the same length-weight conversion, indicating that a nearly fifteen-fold increase in somatic mass occurs between the onset of puberty and the attainment of maximum size. This substantial post-maturity growth is characteristic of teleosts with indeterminate somatic expansion, allowing continued allocation of resources to body maintenance and future fecundity even after reproductive activity has commenced. The protracted growth phase also implies that older, larger females contribute disproportionately to annual egg production, a pattern with important implications for fisheries management and the design of marine protected areas.

Longevity data from tag-recapture studies and otolith age validation indicate that Parore can achieve a maximum lifespan of 24 years [am = 24 years] when reared under natural thermal regimes averaging 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable for a species of its body size and places it among the longest-lived members of the Kyphosidae family, a trait that likely reflects the relatively low natural mortality rates experienced by adults in estuarine and nearshore habitats. Such extended lifespans allow for repeated reproductive episodes across multiple decades, enhancing the potential for population resilience in the face of environmental variability. From a comparative perspective, this longevity is consistent with the slow-life-history syndrome observed in other temperate reef fishes that exhibit delayed maturation, moderate fecundity, and high adult survival.
